text: Kancheepuram Silk sarees are handwoven silk sarees from the temple town of Kancheepuram in Tamil Nadu. They are known for heavy mulberry silk, broad contrasting borders, rich zari work and traditional motifs such as temple towers, checks, stripes and floral buttas. The saree, its border and pallu are typically woven in distinct contrasting colours.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 15 (paraphrased)

text: The geographical area of production covers Kancheepuram town and the surrounding weaving villages of Kancheepuram district, together with adjoining weaving centres in Tiruvannamalai district (and Chengalpattu, formerly part of Kancheepuram district). Sarees woven outside this delimited area may not be sold as Kancheepuram Silk under the GI.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 15 (paraphrased)

text: Only pure mulberry silk yarn is used for warp and weft. The zari is pure silk thread twisted with silver wire and gilded with gold. Yarn is dyed in natural or acid dyes before weaving. Art silk, polyester or tested (imitation) zari are not permitted for a product claiming the Kancheepuram Silk GI.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 15 (paraphrased)

text: Sarees are woven on traditional pit or frame handlooms with jacquard or dobby attachments. The body, border and pallu are woven separately and interlocked by the korvai technique, in which a second weaver often assists. Weaving a single saree typically takes ten to twenty days depending on design complexity.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 15 (paraphrased)

text: The korvai interlocking of contrasting border and body, the use of three-ply mulberry silk giving a heavy, durable fabric, and the pure gold-and-silver zari distinguish Kancheepuram Silk. The joint between body and border is so strong that the border will not separate even if the saree tears.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 15 (paraphrased)

text: Quality is monitored by the applicant weavers' cooperative societies together with the Department of Handlooms and Textiles, Government of Tamil Nadu. An inspection body verifies that registered producers use pure silk and zari and weave within the defined geographical area, and handles misuse of the GI.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 15 (paraphrased)

text: Kancheepuram has been a weaving centre for over four hundred years; weavers of the Devanga and Saliya communities are recorded as settling here under royal patronage. Temple inscriptions and colonial district gazetteers record silk weaving in Kancheepuram as a principal industry of the town.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 15 (paraphrased)

text: Genuine products carry a GI label and logo with the registration details, the name of the authorised user or cooperative society, and silk mark certification. Interlocked korvai borders, a distinct pallu and heavy zari are visual markers; labels state the place of weaving within the GI area.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 15 (paraphrased)

text: Pochampalli Ikat is a handwoven textile of cotton, silk or silk-cotton blend made by the tie-and-dye (ikat) method in Bhoodan Pochampally and nearby villages of Telangana. It is known for geometric diamond and diagonal patterns, with the design dyed into the yarn before weaving rather than printed on the fabric.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 4 (paraphrased)

text: The geographical area of production comprises Pochampally and the surrounding weaving villages of Yadadri Bhuvanagiri district (formerly part of Nalgonda district), including Koyalagudem, Puttapaka, Choutuppal and Siripuram, along with adjoining clusters of Nalgonda district. The GI was registered in 2004-05 when the area was part of Andhra Pradesh.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 4 (paraphrased)

text: Raw materials are mercerised cotton yarn, mulberry silk yarn, or a silk-cotton mix. Yarn is dyed using fast vat, naphthol or natural dyes. Rubber or plastic strips and cotton thread are used for tying sections of the yarn to resist dye in the ikat process.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 4 (paraphrased)

text: Warp and/or weft yarns are marked, tied in bundles and dyed repeatedly so that the untied portions take colour, producing the design on the yarn. The dyed yarns are then carefully aligned on a pit or frame handloom and woven by hand. Single ikat and double ikat (warp and weft) are both practised.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 4 (paraphrased)

text: The design is created entirely in the yarn before weaving, giving a characteristic feathered or blurred edge to the geometric motifs. The precise alignment of pre-dyed warp and weft on the handloom cannot be reproduced by printing or powerloom weaving, which makes Pochampalli Ikat distinctive.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 4 (paraphrased)

text: The Pochampally Handloom Weavers' Cooperative Society and the Department of Handlooms and Textiles of the state government act as the inspection structure, checking that authorised users follow the tie-and-dye method on handlooms within the registered geographical area.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 4 (paraphrased)

text: Ikat weaving in Pochampally is traced to the early twentieth century, drawing on the older telia rumal tradition of the region. Pochampally is also historically known as Bhoodan Pochampally after the land-gift movement of 1951. It was among the first Indian products to receive GI protection.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 4 (paraphrased)

text: Authentic Pochampalli Ikat carries the GI logo, the name of the authorised weaver or cooperative, and handloom mark. The design is visible equally on both sides of the fabric, and motif edges show the slight irregularity typical of hand tie-dyed yarn; printed imitations show the design only on the face.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 4 (paraphrased)

text: Banaras Brocades and Sarees are handwoven silk fabrics and sarees with intricate brocade (zari) patterns, produced in Varanasi and surrounding districts of Uttar Pradesh. Varieties include katan, kora, organza, georgette and shattir, with motifs such as kalga, bel, jaal, buta and Mughal-inspired floral designs.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 99 (paraphrased)

text: The geographical area of production covers six districts of Uttar Pradesh: Varanasi, Mirzapur, Chandauli, Bhadohi, Jaunpur and Azamgarh. Products woven outside these districts, including those made in other states, are not entitled to be sold as Banaras Brocades and Sarees under the GI.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 99 (paraphrased)

text: Raw materials are mulberry silk yarn (often in katan or twisted form), cotton for some varieties, and zari of gold or silver coated silk or copper thread. Dyeing is done in hank form before weaving. Synthetic yarn substitutes are not part of the registered product specification.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 99 (paraphrased)

text: Weaving is done on pit or frame handlooms fitted with jacquard or naksha (draw) devices that lift warp threads to create brocade figures. Extra-weft techniques such as kadhua and fekua are used to insert zari motifs. A heavy brocade saree may take from fifteen days to several months to weave.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 99 (paraphrased)

text: The kadhua technique, in which each motif is woven separately by hand with extra weft, together with dense zari work and the traditional design vocabulary of Varanasi, distinguishes Banaras brocades from machine-made imitations, which cannot reproduce the hand-inserted motifs.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 99 (paraphrased)

text: The applicant associations of weavers and traders, supported by the Office of the Development Commissioner (Handlooms) and the Weavers' Service Centre, Varanasi, oversee authorised users and check that products are handwoven within the six GI districts using the specified materials.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 99 (paraphrased)

text: Varanasi has been a centre of silk weaving for centuries; references to Banaras textiles appear in ancient texts, and brocade weaving flourished under Mughal patronage. Colonial records describe the Banaras brocade industry as one of the most important handicraft industries of the United Provinces.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 99 (paraphrased)

text: Genuine products carry the GI logo with the authorised user's details and the Handloom Mark. The reverse side of a handwoven kadhua brocade shows no loose floats between motifs, while powerloom imitations show long cut floats; labels name the weaving district within the GI area.
source: IP India GI Journal, Application No. 99 (paraphrased)
